classification.difficultyReason: The diagonal PR is drawn and the parts are signposted: cosine rule for PR, cosine rule again for angle PSR, then a sum of two SAS triangle areas. A prepared student makes few decisions. The demand is the chain of three linked procedures, which includes carrying the PR value forward and splitting the quadrilateral into two triangles. That is slightly more than a single-step area question. It is not harder than choosing between sine and cosine rules, since the method for each part is stated.

classification.difficultyReason: The parts are heavily scaffolded. Part a applies the supplied angle-sum formula and divides by 5. Part b uses base angles of an isosceles triangle. Part c is a direct SAS area calculation using the 108° angle from part a with two sides of 6 cm. The only decisions are finding the included angle and recognising the equal sides from the marks. There is no diagonal-length or cosine-rule step, so it is more than plain substitution but below a task needing a sine-rule calculation.
